title: Fix the above bug using `collect(Collectors.toList())` instead of mutating a shared collection.
shortTitle: Fix the parallel-stream collection bug using collect(Collectors.toList())

s1_definition.profdef: Replacing the shared-mutable-list `forEach(list::add)` with `collect(Collectors.toList())` makes the stream framework accumulate results thread-safely. Each thread collects into its own container and the framework merges them, eliminating the race.
s1_definition.analogy: Instead of all clerks writing into one ledger at once, each clerk keeps their own page and a supervisor staples the pages together at the end. No collisions.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use `collect(toList())` so the framework handles thread-safe accumulation — never mutate a shared collection in parallel.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Replacing the shared-mutable-list `forEach(list::add)` with `collect(Collectors.toList())` makes the stream framework accumulate results thread-safely. Each thread collects into its own container and the framework merges them, eliminating the race.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Instead of all clerks writing into one ledger at once, each clerk keeps their own page and a supervisor staples the pages together at the end. No collisions.

**One line to remember:** Use `collect(toList())` so the framework handles thread-safe accumulation — never mutate a shared collection in parallel.

sections.s2_technical:
`source.parallelStream().filter(...).collect(Collectors.toList())` lets the stream pipeline manage result accumulation. For a parallel stream the framework uses per-thread intermediate containers and a combiner to merge them, so there is no shared mutable state and no race. The result is correct and deterministic in content regardless of thread count.

This is the idiomatic, side-effect-free way to gather stream results. `collect` is designed around the supplier, accumulator, and combiner contract precisely so it works correctly in parallel. The fix replaces the imperative forEach-add with a declarative collector.

The senior nuance is that this embodies the side-effect-free principle: streams should produce results through return values, not by mutating external state. The collector's combiner step is what makes parallel collection safe, which is why you must never hand-roll parallel accumulation with a plain collection. If order must match the source in parallel, toList preserves encounter order for an ordered stream; for unordered sources I would note that. collect is the single correct answer to parallel result gathering.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — After the shared-ArrayList race at the National Bank of India, the fix must collect filtered transactions correctly even in parallel.

This is exactly what collect with toList does — it accumulates thread-safely and returns a complete, correct list.

The code defines a `SafeCollectService using collect and a demo verifying the correct size.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: one hundred thousand integers, filtering the fifty thousand even ones.

Step 1: parallelStream splits the source across worker threads.

Step 2: Each thread filters its chunk and collects into its own intermediate list via the collector's accumulator.

Step 3: The framework merges the per-thread lists with the collector's combiner.

Step 4: The final list always has exactly fifty thousand elements, correct and deterministic on every run.

```
INFO: run 1 → size=50000 (always 50000, correct)
INFO: run 2 → size=50000 (always 50000, correct)
INFO: run 3 → size=50000 (always 50000, correct)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The fix for the parallel-stream race is to stop mutating a shared collection and instead use collect with Collectors toList. When I collect, the stream framework manages the accumulation for me: on a parallel stream it gives each worker thread its own intermediate container, fills them independently, and then merges them with the collector's combiner step. Because no thread ever touches shared mutable state, there is no race, and the result is correct and deterministic on every run.

This is the idiomatic, side-effect-free way to gather stream results, and it is exactly what collect was designed for — the supplier, accumulator, and combiner contract is what makes parallel collection safe. At the National Bank of India this turned the intermittently-corrupt transaction list into one that always has precisely the expected count.

The senior point I stress is that the correct instinct is never to hand-roll parallel accumulation by synchronizing a plain list, but to let collect do it. It embodies the principle that streams should produce results through return values rather than by mutating external state. I also note that for an ordered source toList preserves encounter order even in parallel, so the content and ordering are both correct. collect is the single right answer to safe parallel result gathering.
